381.quote_or_event: After the martyrdom of his father Guru Arjan, Guru Hargobind took up two swords at his succession, standing for temporal (miri) and spiritual (piri) authority. He trained in arms, built up a Sikh army, fortified his towns, built the Lohgarh fort near Amritsar, and in 1609 founded the Akal Takht as a seat where both the spiritual and the temporal affairs of the community could be settled.
381.explanation: Guru Hargobind gave the Sikh community the means of a self-governing body, with an army, fortifications and a seat of authority, alongside its spiritual life.
381.tie_back: The Kural lists army, people, resources, counsel, allies and fortification as the parts of a strong state; Guru Hargobind's miri-piri reforms gave the young Panth several of these same limbs.
381._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on building the structural strength of a polity; Guru Hargobind's forces served to defend a faith community, not a kingdom, and the Kural's six-part list is not reproduced item by item.

382.quote_or_event: “One who does not frighten anyone, and who is not afraid of anyone else - says Nanak, listen, mind: call him spiritually wise.”
382.explanation: In his saloks Guru Tegh Bahadur defines the truly wise person as one who neither intimidates others nor is intimidated by them.
382.tie_back: The Kural names fearlessness and wisdom among the four qualities a ruler must never lack; Guru Tegh Bahadur joins the same two, making fearlessness itself a mark of wisdom.
382.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahala 9, Salok 16, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
382._accuracy_note: Covers fearlessness and wisdom but not generosity or energy, and it describes the spiritually wise person in general, not a king.

383.quote_or_event: “Those who remain awake and aware are saved, while those who sleep are plundered.”
383.explanation: Guru Amar Das warns that only those who stay alert are protected, while the careless sleeper is robbed of everything of value.
383.tie_back: The Kural says sleepless vigilance must never leave those who rule; Guru Amar Das gives the same warning that whoever stops keeping watch loses what they hold.
383.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 34, Siree Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
383._accuracy_note: Next-best: the vigilance meant is spiritual watchfulness against vice and maya, not a ruler's promptness, and learning and resolve, the Kural's other two qualities, are not covered.

384.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
384.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, in a hymn included in the Guru Granth Sahib, says the true hero is one who fights for righteousness and does not abandon the field even when cut to pieces.
384.tie_back: The Kural joins never swerving from righteousness with a valour and honour that never falls short; Kabir's hero is defined by exactly that union of dharma and unyielding courage.
384.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
384._accuracy_note: Strong fit on righteousness joined with courage; the verse concerns the spiritual warrior in general rather than a king's duty to remove wrongdoing from the land, and other translators render 'deen' as the poor or helpless.

385.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
385.explanation: Guru Nanak says the true path is to live by honest labour and to share part of what one earns, the basis of the Sikh ideals of kirat karni and vand chhakna.
385.tie_back: The Kural's theory of government runs from producing and gathering wealth to distributing it wisely; Guru Nanak gives the same cycle of earning and sharing at the level of the individual householder.
385.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
385._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the earn-and-share ethic parallels producing and distributing wealth, but it is personal ethics, not public finance, and says nothing about collecting or safeguarding revenue.

386.quote_or_event: “Sweetness and humility, O Nanak, are the essence of virtue and goodness.”
386.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak names sweetness of manner and humility as the very essence of every good quality.
386.tie_back: The Kural praises the king who is never harsh of speech; Guru Nanak makes the same gentleness of manner the essence of virtue.
386.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
386._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it matches the Kural's avoidance of harsh speech, but not its main point that the ruler be easy for his people to approach.

387.quote_or_event: “The Lord lovingly embraces whoever comes to the Lord's Sanctuary - this is the way of the Lord and Master.”
387.explanation: Guru Arjan says it is the innate nature (birad) of the Master to take into His embrace anyone who comes seeking refuge.
387.tie_back: The Kural praises the ruler who gives kindly and protects those who come to him; Guru Arjan describes the divine Master whose defining way is exactly such protection of all who seek shelter.
387.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 544, Raag Bihaagraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
387._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the verse describes God, not a human ruler, and says nothing of kind speech or of the world following the ruler's word.

388.quote_or_event: “That king sits upon the throne, who is worthy of that throne.”
388.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that a throne belongs only to the one who is worthy of it; Sikh thought reserves the title of True King (sacha patshah) for God alone.
388.tie_back: The Kural says a king who rules justly and protects his people is regarded as divine; Guru Nanak likewise makes the right to rule depend on worthiness, though he does not grant any king divine status.
388.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1088, Raag Maaroo, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
388._accuracy_note: Partial: the shared idea is that legitimacy rests on worth, but Sikhism would not have people regard any ruler as God, and the line is often read inwardly as the throne of spiritual wisdom.

389.quote_or_event: “The kings are tigers, and their officials are dogs; they go out and awaken the sleeping people to harass them.”
389.explanation: In Vaar Malaar Guru Nanak speaks a famously bitter truth about the rulers of his day, comparing kings to tigers and their officials to dogs that prey on ordinary people.
389.tie_back: The Kural praises the king gracious enough to bear words that are bitter to his ears; Guru Nanak's verse is an example of the bitter, unwelcome truth that a good ruler ought to be able to hear.
389.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1288, Raag Malaar (Vaar Malaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
389._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Gurbani here speaks the bitter word to power rather than praising a ruler who accepts it, so it illustrates the Kural's point only from the critic's side.

390.quote_or_event: “Now, the Merciful Lord has issued His Command. Let no one chase after and attack anyone else. Let all abide in peace, under this Benevolent Rule.”
390.explanation: Guru Arjan describes halemi raj, a gentle and benevolent rule under the merciful Lord's command, in which no one harasses another and all live in peace.
390.tie_back: The Kural calls the ruler who joins generosity, compassion, just rule and care for the people the light among kings; Guru Arjan's halemi raj is Sikhism's picture of such compassionate, peaceful rule.
390.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 74, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
390._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on benevolent, protective rule; the rule meant is God's, and commentators such as Sahib Singh read it inwardly as humility's reign in the heart, not as a human king's government.
